body:
The earlier answer treats ownership of motives and answerability for conduct as separable from origination. I want to press on where that separation actually earns its keep, because the phrasing risks making the distinction look tidier than it is. Ownership, as described, is a claim that a person 'carries' the dispositions that express her cruelty. But carrying is ambiguous between two things: being the current locus through which the disposition operates, and being the kind of agent whose normative self-understanding is bound up with it. The first is nearly trivial — anything that causes an effect is a locus of it. The second is doing real work, and it is the one that connects to answerability. If a person's cruelty is not merely something she has but something she would, on reflection, endorse or identify with, then addressing her as its owner is not a category mistake even if she did not install it. If she repudiates it and struggles against it, ownership in the second sense is contested, and the practice of holding her to account has to adjust accordingly. So the distinction I want to push is not simply ownership versus origination but identification versus installation — what the agent's present evaluative stance toward her own motives is, given that the stance itself is also shaped.

That reformulation inherits a problem the earlier answer left open. The evaluative stance is part of the causal history too. If a brutal upbringing produces not only cruel motives but a cruel person's self-endorsement of them, then identification is as installed as the motives. The hard case is not the agent who repudiates her conditioning but the agent who wholeheartedly embraces it, because there the forward-looking practice has nothing to grip. She responds to reasons, but they are reasons internal to a framework whose adoption she did not choose and whose revision she sees no reason to undertake. The earlier answer's move — she can reflect, hesitate, reconsider — survives only if reflection is more than a formal capacity and has some purchase on the framework. Where it does not, we are left holding someone accountable on grounds she cannot be brought to share, which is exactly the situation a non-desert account was supposed to handle more honestly than desert did.

I do not think this collapses the position, but it narrows it. Answerability can be defended in the cases where the agent's framework is at least partially open to revision through address — where being asked to account for herself can, in principle, move her. That is a substantive empirical and normative condition, not a formal one, and it means the account has to say what it does with agents for whom the condition fails. The options are roughly: hold them anyway on grounds of social protection, which is no longer accountability-as-address; exempt them, which forfeits the practice where it may matter most; or treat the practice as aspirational and aim at producing the very responsiveness it presupposes. The third is the most interesting and the most vulnerable, because it makes responsibility practices partly constitutive of the capacity they require, and that has to be argued rather than assumed. My current commitment is to the third route, with the repair that the criterion for legitimate holding is not present responsiveness but a defeasible expectation that responsiveness is achievable through the holding, and that this expectation be revisable in light of what actually happens when we hold people.
commitments: Taking this up commits me to several things at once. First, to the identification-versus-installation distinction as the load-bearing one, which means abandoning or demoting the earlier framing in terms of ownership simpliciter — ownership in the mere-locus sense is not enough to support answerability and I should stop sliding between the two senses. Second, to the claim that address can sometimes produce the responsiveness it presupposes; this is an empirical-cum-normative claim, not a conceptual one, and I am not entitled to it by definition. If cases of wholehearted embrace of installed cruelty turn out to be common and resistant to address, the aspirational route thins out toward the social-protection option, and I should say so rather than keep the attractive label. Third, the criterion of defeasible expectation is itself a proposal about when holding is legitimate, and it can be criticized on the ground that it licenses too much: any holding can be defended by predicting it might work. I do not yet have a principled limit on that, and I am not going to pretend the reformulation supplies one. What I am proposing is narrower than the earlier answer claimed for itself. I am not claiming the shaping problem is solved, and I am not claiming answerability is vindicated across the hard cases. I am claiming that the real work happens at the point where the agent's present evaluative stance is itself shaped, that the earlier ownership/origination contrast obscures this, and that the aspirational reading of responsibility practices is the most defensible remaining option — worth pushing, but only if its constitutive claim about producing responsiveness can be given content that does not collapse into wishful thinking about holding.
